author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, the four nitrogenous bases, and the hydrogen bonds between base pairs — and describe how they assemble into the double helix.

Students will apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C) to determine the sequence of one strand given the sequence of the other, and explain why these specific pairings occur (two hydrogen bonds for A-T, three for G-C).
Students will describe the antiparallel orientation of the two strands of DNA and explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of each sugar-phosphate backbone determines this arrangement.
Students will trace the action of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork, identifying which enzyme performs which function.

Students will explain why DNA replication produces a leading strand synthesized continuously and a lagging strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, relating this asymmetry to the unidirectional 5'-to-3' activity of DNA polymerase on antiparallel templates.
Students will articulate why DNA replication is described as semiconservative, and predict the composition of daughter molecules after one and two rounds of replication.

modules.description: Introduce DNA as a ladder-like polymer with repeating sugar-phosphate backbones and inward-facing complementary bases.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone and base-pair rungs in a schematic representation.
Associate color-coded bases with their one-letter abbreviations.
Explain that DNA is a polymer with repeating structural units.
instructions: Observe the ladder-like model before any twisting occurs.
Use the labels to connect each colored base with its letter and pairing partner.

clips.changeMeaning: The schematic DNA ladder, backbone labels, and base-pair key appear together to establish the basic structural vocabulary before adding geometric complexity.
clips.narration: DNA is a polymer made of two backbones with nitrogenous bases projecting inward. This ladder view helps us see the repeating pattern of the molecule.

clips.changeMeaning: The ladder is subtly highlighted to draw attention to the repeating backbone and the inward-facing rungs that represent base pairs.
clips.narration: Each rung represents a pair of bases. The bases are arranged in a specific pattern that will determine how the strands interact in the double helix.

modules.description: Transform the schematic ladder into the familiar double helix and compare the two representations.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize that the ladder representation maps onto the three-dimensional double helix.
Observe how two backbones twist around a common axis.
Notice the helical stacking and visible grooves as geometric features of DNA.
instructions: Switch attention from the flat ladder to the helical form.
Rotate the model to compare the interior base pairs and outer backbones.

clips.changeMeaning: The helical DNA model appears with a mapping note, helping students connect the earlier ladder depiction to the three-dimensional structure.
clips.narration: Real DNA forms a double helix. The two backbones spiral around a common axis, and the base pairs stack inside the helix.

clips.changeMeaning: A gentle rotation and orbit are added so students can observe the spiral geometry from multiple viewing angles and notice the repeating helical form.
clips.narration: As you rotate the molecule, notice that the ladder shape has been twisted into a compact helix.

modules.description: Label the 5' and 3' ends and show that the two DNA strands run in opposite directions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify 5' and 3' ends on each strand.
Explain antiparallel arrangement as opposite strand polarity.
Relate backbone directionality to the overall orientation of DNA.
instructions: Follow the arrow markers along each backbone.
Use the terminal labels to determine which end is 5' and which is 3'.

clips.changeMeaning: Terminal labels and the antiparallel note appear so students can connect strand polarity to the physical ends of the molecule.
clips.narration: The two strands run in opposite directions. One strand runs 5' to 3', while the complementary strand runs 3' to 5'.

clips.changeMeaning: The helix is slowly rotated to let students verify the opposite orientation of the strand labels from different viewpoints.
clips.narration: This antiparallel arrangement is a defining property of DNA and is forced by the chemistry of the sugar-phosphate backbone.

modules.description: Students complete a missing complementary strand and see hydrogen-bond counts for correct pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply A-T and G-C pairing rules to build a complementary strand.
Infer the complementary sequence from a template strand.
Relate pair identity to hydrogen-bond number and pairing stability.
instructions: Drag the loose bases to the empty strand to complete the sequence.
Check the hydrogen-bond indicators after each correct placement.

clips.changeMeaning: The complementary-strand activity and base palette appear, giving students a hands-on sequence-building task with pairing guidance.
clips.narration: Use complementary base-pairing rules to complete the missing strand. Adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine.

clips.changeMeaning: The complementary strand is configured to respond to student placements, supporting immediate feedback on base-pair accuracy and sequence completion.
clips.narration: Correct base choices will snap into place and reveal the hydrogen-bond pattern associated with each pair.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: Replication Fork and Enzyme Actions
modules.description: Show helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase working at a replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase as the enzyme that unwinds DNA.
Describe how single-strand binding proteins stabilize exposed templates.
Recognize DNA polymerase as the enzyme that extends new DNA strands and ligase as the enzyme that seals fragments.
instructions: Watch the fork open and identify each protein by name.
Pay attention to the order in which the replication proteins appear.

clips.changeMeaning: The full replication fork and enzyme set appear together, establishing the cast of molecular machines before showing their coordinated action.
clips.narration: At the replication fork, helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins stabilize the exposed DNA, polymerase builds new strands, and ligase seals breaks.

clips.changeMeaning: The enzyme positions shift to suggest movement along the fork, helping students connect each enzyme to its active location and task.
clips.narration: These enzymes do not all do the same job. Helicase leads the opening, polymerase extends DNA, and ligase joins completed pieces.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Leading and Lagging Strand Synthesis
modules.description: Demonstrate continuous leading-strand synthesis and discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis with Okazaki fragments.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why DNA polymerase synthesizes only in the 5' to 3' direction.
Differentiate continuous leading-strand synthesis from discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.
Describe how Okazaki fragments are later joined by DNA ligase.
instructions: Compare the two template strands and the direction of synthesis.
Observe how fragments accumulate on the lagging strand before being sealed.

clips.changeMeaning: The active fork appears with pre-positioned leading and lagging strand models, establishing the contrast between continuous and fragmentary synthesis.
clips.narration: Because DNA polymerase can extend only in the 5' to 3' direction, one new strand is made continuously while the other is made in short fragments.

clips.changeMeaning: The Okazaki fragments and ligase shift into tighter alignment to visually indicate fragment joining into a continuous lagging strand.
clips.narration: These short DNA pieces are called Okazaki fragments. DNA ligase seals the gaps between them to complete the strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Distinct colors are reinforced on each strand so students can remember which pathway is continuous and which is discontinuous during summary narration.
clips.narration: The asymmetry comes from antiparallel templates and the one-way chemistry of DNA polymerase.

modules.description: Predict and verify the products of one and two rounds of DNA replication.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define semiconservative replication in terms of strand inheritance.
Predict the strand composition of daughter DNA after one replication cycle.
Predict the strand composition after a second replication cycle.
instructions: Compare the parental strands with the newly synthesized strands.
Make a prediction before the second replication round is revealed.

components.text: Each daughter keeps one old strand

clips.changeMeaning: The parental molecule splits into two daughter molecules with distinct old and new strand colors, demonstrating that each product retains one parental strand.
clips.narration: DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter molecule contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

clips.changeMeaning: The second round of replication products appear, allowing students to verify the predicted mixture of hybrid and fully new molecules after two replication cycles.
clips.narration: After a second round, some molecules remain hybrid while others are entirely newly synthesized. This pattern confirms the semiconservative model.
